sweep_summary: Gothic (goth1244) is in the catalog as fixed initial stress (Wright 1910 §33). The two title-works with stress in the title are both De Gruyter paywalled articles that could not be opened by any open route (DOI landing returns a bot challenge with no abstract; Unpaywall is_oa=false; Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex/CORE/archive.org/Google Scholar/academia.edu gave nothing): Suzuki 1982 (metrical approach to Gothic reduplication) is unclear/possibly stress-relevant (the stress of the reduplicating syllable is a known issue), priority medium; Pierce 2003 (Prosody and Sievers' Law) is, on the evidence of the author's companion 2006 JGL abstract and Barrack's 2010 reply (both read and saved), about syllable structure/weight, not word-stress placement, priority low. The most useful new first-hand statement obtained is the verbatim publisher abstract of Bennett 1970 'The Stress Patterns of Gothic' (PMLA), saved to primary stress fixed on word-initial syllables (roots, reduplicating syllables, prefixes incl. un-), secondary stress on second compound members, preverbs as proclitics; it confirms and refines the catalog's classification but, being abstract-only, does not supersede Wright 1910 as deciding source (full text is the high-priority acquisition, Cambridge Core/JSTOR). Streitberg 1920 §36/§231 (already held by the project, read) independently confirms initial stress with verbal compounds stressing the stem. and updated in the goth1244 our files.

new_statements.quote: In Gothic, as in Proto-Germanic, primary word stress was fixed on word-initial syllables, including roots, reduplicating syllables, and prefixes; the Gothic negative-pejorative prefix un- appears to have been no exception to the rule. Secondary word stress occurred initially on second immediate constituents of compounds and quasi-compounds; the stress of gudhŨs ‘temple’ and faurhāh ‘curtain’ was not exceptional. Weak word stress fell medially on vowels between syllables bearing other degrees of stress and on syllable-forming suffixes directly following primary or secondary stress; finally, weak word stress occurred on syllable-forming endings.
new_statements.citation: Bennett, William H. 1970. The Stress Patterns of Gothic. PMLA 85(3): 463-472. doi:10.2307/1261448
new_statements.locator: author's published abstract (Cambridge Core citation_abstract), article pp. 463-472; full text not read
new_statements.reading: Fixed primary stress on the word-initial syllable (root, reduplicating syllable, or prefix, including un-); secondary stress on the second member of compounds; weak stress on medial vowels and endings; verbal preverbs analysed as proclitics with secondary phrase stress (ga- weak), so the verb root keeps primary word stress. This is the dedicated study of Gothic stress and agrees with the catalog's 'fixed' initial coding while adding a graded stress hierarchy.

new_statements.quote: § 33. The rule for the accentuation of uncompounded words is the same in Gothic as in the oldest period of the other Germanic languages, viz. the chief stress fell upon the first syllable, and always remained there even when suffixes and inflexional endings followed it, as áudags, blessed; niman, to take; reikinōn, to rule; the preterite of reduplicated verbs, as laílōt : lētan, to let; haíháit : háitan, to call; [...] The position of the secondary stress in trisyllabic and polysyllabic words fluctuated in Gothic, and with the present state of our knowledge of the subject it is impossible to formulate any hard and fast rules concerning it.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's fixed: initial syllable coding and as Bennett 1970 (initial primary stress). Adds: verbal prefixes do not take the chief stress (the verb root does), which is the same fact Bennett analyses as proclitic preverbs; nominal compounds keep initial stress; secondary stress fluctuates and cannot be stated by rule (Bennett places it on the second member of compounds, so Wright is more agnostic but not in conflict).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chief (primary) stress on the first syllable of every uncompounded word, staying there whatever suffixes or inflexional endings follow (including the reduplicating syllable of reduplicated preterites, laílōt, haíháit); nominal and adjectival compounds also stress the first element (§34: frakunþs, gaskafts, unmahts, ufkunþi, usfilh, piudangardi); in compound verbs the second element, i.e. the verb, carries the chief stress (atlagjan, duginnan, frakunnan, gaqiman, usfulljan). Wright (§32, p. 15) frames this as the prim. Germanic confinement of the chief accent to the first syllable after the Verner's-law period.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §33 p. 15: 'The position of the secondary stress in trisyllabic and polysyllabic words fluctuated in Gothic, and with the present state of our knowledge of the subject it is impossible to formulate any hard and fast rules concerning it.'
new_statements.exceptions: §34 pp. 15-16: 'But in compound verbs the second element had the chief stress, as atlagjan, to lay on; duginnan, to begin; frakunnan, to despise; gaqiman, to assemble; usfulljan, to fulfil. When, however, the first element of a compound verb was separated from the verb by one or more particles, it had the chief stress, as gá-u-hva-sēhvi, Mark viii. 23; diz-uh-þan-sat, Mark xvi. 8.' Contrast pairs ándahafts 'answer' vs andháfjan 'to answer', ándanēms vs andniman (§33-34 p. 16). Wright's acute marks (áu, aí) are his vowel-quality notation, not stress marks.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Biblical (Wulfilian) Gothic as attested in the Gospel manuscripts; Wright's §34 cites Mark viii. 23 and xvi. 8. No dialect distinctions arise.

new_statements.quote: Traditionally it is agreed that Gothic words had initial stress (cf. Krause 1968: 70-72; Jellinek 1926). [fn. 4:] In words with some prefixes the main stress does not fall on the absolute initial syllable, but on the initial syllable of the stem. [...] The words in (8) are assigned initial stress. According to the representations in (8), however, Gothic words should also have secondary stress. Evidence for such secondary stress in Gothic non-compounded words is less clear (cf. Jellinek 1926: 53). We will assume that there was no secondary stress in Gothic.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (Wright 1910 §33: chief stress on the first syllable) and as Bennett 1970 (fixed initial primary stress): agrees on fixed initial main stress. Adds (i) a formal weight-sensitive foot construction (Prokosch's Law: initial heavy syllable = two light syllables as one foot) that leaves main stress initial, (ii) the stem-initial stress of certain prefixed words (compatible with Wright §34 / Bennett's proclitic preverbs), and (iii) an explicit assumption of no secondary stress in non-compounds, where Wright says the position of secondary stress in polysyllables 'fluctuated' and Bennett posits weak medial stress; this is a stance on unclear evidence, not a diff…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word stress in Gothic is initial: the stress rules (6)-(7) build left-headed feet from the left edge (a non-final heavy syllable projects a right foot boundary, so an initial heavy syllable or an initial pair of light syllables forms the first foot, per Prokosch's Law) and the head of the leftmost foot carries main stress, i.e. the first syllable of the word; with certain (non-cyclic) prefixes main stress falls on the stem-initial syllable instead of the absolute word-initial syllable. Syllable weight shapes foot structure but never moves the main stress off the initial syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: The iterative footing would predict secondary stresses, but Calabrese states that evidence for secondary stress in non-compounded Gothic words is unclear (Jellinek 1926: 53) and assumes there was NO secondary stress in Gothic, removing it formally by conflation (only the initial main-stress foot survives); footnote 5 contrasts Old English, which 'most probably had secondary stress'. Compounds are not discussed.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 4: in words with some prefixes main stress falls on the initial syllable of the stem, not the prefix (handled by treating those prefixes as non-cyclic morphemes). No lexical exceptions otherwise.
new_statements.identity_note: Biblical (Wulfilian) Gothic as attested in the manuscript corpus; the paper analyses the ja-stem noun and class I weak verb alternations (Sievers' Law) and states the word-stress/foot system as the prosodic basis of that analysis; no dialect distinctions.

sources.note: §36 Anhang '2. Betonung' (pp. 65-66; the scanned text): no direct testimony for Gothic accent, but no doubt that the Common Germanic principle held, i.e. the word accent in native words fell on the first syllable; the only exception is verbal compounds, which stress the stem syllable, not the prefix (§231). Nominal compounds with monosyllabic first member show the pattern stressed-unstressed-stressed (gabaurþai, gaqumþai); compounds with un- have double main stress. §231 (pp. 160-161, the scanned text): Germanic nominal compounds accent the first member, verbal compounds the second; this rule…
